utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please take the affirmation card and read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Thanks a lot. Sorry for that. Today we have another witness, and while this witness is under protective measures I will just call not the witness by name but by Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Witness, you have been recalled to deal with only one document which the Prosecution served on the Defence after you did conclude your evidence in this Tribunal on the 8th of November last year. And for that reason, while it is the Defence that has recalled the witness, I will then give the floor to Mr. Vasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to all present in the courtroom. Good morning to the witness. I would kindly ask you to pause before you provide answers to my questions so that we would leave sufficient time for the interpreters and also so that your voice wouldn't carry via my microphone, having in mind the measures that you enjoy. This will be a short cross-examination, having in mind the topic we need to cover. Witness, in April 1992, do you remember having given a statement to any state bodies or commissions dealing with searches for missing persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't remember having given any such statement to a state body or to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the aid of the usher, I wanted to provide a copy of the statement for you, and we received it from our learned friends. Could you please verify whether this is the statement you have actually given. This is ERN number 0202-7813 in the English. Witness, please take a look at the statement, and tell me whether you remember having given this statement. You have the Croatian version, I presume. On the 15th of April, 1992, do you remember having given this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: When we left Vukovar in 1992, we were put in a hotel. There were various journalists coming to see us, and they received information from us. I was in the same facility. In those very rooms, there were five or six women there, and there were several journalists that went through the facility and they used to note something down in the notebooks. But I have never provided a statement in the sense that I was sat down with someone and someone was typing my statement. Later on this was typed, but I don't know by whom. Perhaps they did that from their recollection. There is no signature of mine here, and I can't state that I have given this statement. At least in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, some of the contents is what you believe you had said to the journalists, but as concerns some other portions of the statement, that is something you cannot recall. Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: You are. Since there were several people in the room when they came to see us, they wanted to know how we had left Vukovar, who was in the hospital, and so on and so forth. And then various women said various things. Therefore, I can't say who the journalist was, and given the circumstances and my mental state, I don't really know what it was that I could have said. Had she noted down my name and then something I had said, then I would be able to say that those were my words. Otherwise I can't claim that I have given this statement in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony here you stated that on the morning, as you were walking through the corridors, that you saw a doctor, but you also added that you can't distinguish clearly between Dr. Stanojevic and Dr. Manojlovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please make a pause before you answer so you give me the time necessary to turn off my microphone? In the statement we are discussing, which, as you say, was noted down by the journalists, one can read that that morning you saw Dr. Manojlovic. Is it possible that you saw Dr. Manojlovic walking along the corridor, pointing at various people and telling -- or rather, informing some people who was Croat who was Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I abide by the statement I had given that one of the doctors was pointing out people, saying this one was Serb, this one was Croat. And here one can read that this was Dr. Manojlovic, who was doing it. But that could have been said by anyone else of the people who were present when the statement was taken. I can claim with certainty that it was one of the two, although I am uncertain which one. And I wasn't certain at the time either. It states here that it was Dr. Manojlovic. Perhaps one of the women knew him better than I did, and then she said that that was his name. But I abide by what I had stated in my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you state to the journalist what can be read from the statement, that Dr. Manojlovic was going from one wounded person to the next, together with a captain, whose name I don't know, and that they were compiling is a list of Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I stated something different. I stated that passing through the corridor, connecting the two parts of the hospital, and that corridor is underground, as we were going out there was one of the doctors there. Whether it was Dr. Manojlovic or Dr. Stanojevic, I don't know. And there was a JNA captain with him. Even then I didn't know his name was Mrksic because I didn't know JNA captains then. But some soldiers came up to him and they addressed him with "Comrade Mrksic." That is what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering the questions posed by my learned friend on page 1186, you stated something quite different, that it wasn't the soldiers who addressed him with "Comrade Mrksic," but rather that the physician addressed him with "Comrade Mrksic." Do you remember having said that, and that is quite different from what you are saying today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: It is not different. The doctor was there, and there were soldiers there, and both the doctor and the soldiers addressed him that way. I heard that particular name in passing. And this doctor addressed him that way as well. I don't know which one, but one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will read out that portion of the transcript, since there is no mention of any soldiers there. Perhaps then you can clarify whether you remember having said that only the doctor was there and that you didn't know whether it was Stanojevic or Manojlovic. That was page 1186, lines 3 to 7. Excuse me, to 9. "[In English] On the morning of the 20th as I was passing down that corridor, there was a doctor, I'm not quite sure which one it was. But I believe it was Dr. Stanojevic. He was there with a high military official whose rank I didn't know, because I don't know about these things. He spoke to him, however, saying Comrade Mrksic. They were walking together down the corridor, and this doctor, who, by the way, hails from Vukovar, and he knew most of the patients, was saying this one is ours and this one isn't." [Interpretation] Do you remember having said this in your answers to one of the questions of my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but the hospital was full. There were soldiers there and lots of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please go back to the statement? Would you agree with me that in the statement that mentions your name, and I won't mention it because of the protective measures you enjoy, in one of its sentences one can read the following: "As I was going from the kitchen towards the exit, and I was passing through the wounded or between the wounded, Dr. Manojlovic was going from one wounded person to the next with a captain whose name I don't know, and they were compiling a list of people specifying who was Serb and who was Croat."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: This is what can be read from the statement, but perhaps it wasn't me who said that. I'm telling you that there were many women in the room, and the journalist was jotting things down in his notebook, and then he compiled the statement. What I can say now is that this is the first time I've seen this statement, and I can't claim that this indeed is my statement. If she put my name there, it could be that she remembered my name out of all the women and she quoted it here. But this is not a type of statement for which I could say that, yes, it corresponds to every word I say. Any woman who was present in the room could have said that and the journalist put the statement together, there is no signature, we didn't know who wrote it, and I can't be specific as to the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the other persons present provide their names or were you the only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: She asked all of us for our names, and I can tell you five other women who were there with me, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That won't be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Miroslav Radic's Defence will have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence will have no additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, I had forgotten that. Quite some time since I was in the courtroom, so sorry for that. Further re-examination by Ms. Tuma:

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you -- if I understood you right, this was the first time that you have seen this document arriving here at The Hague this time. Is that correctly understood from me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Have anyone before you arriving here to The Hague this time read out this statement to you before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last question, please, to the witness. Why did you not mention that even the soldiers also did address the JNA officer as "Comrade Mrksic" before? Why haven't you mentioned that earlier on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-013 [Recalled]
utterances.text: I get somewhat confused here, and anxious. I can't explain any better than that. If we were to discuss this outside of the courtroom with my eyes closed, I can be very specific as to what had happened, but as soon as I enter the courtroom I don't feel very comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No further question, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Tuma. I'm pleased to be able to say that your questioning has concluded. We are very grateful that you have been able to return at the request of the Defence to deal with this one further issue. We thank you once again for the assistance that you have given to the Tribunal, and you may now return to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The court officer will assist you to leave the court. We must wait, for your protection, for these shutters to close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, are there other matters you wish to raise at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that is the admission of the 92 bis material based on a decision from this Trial Chamber on the 21st of October, 2005. Can I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to this decision as said from the 21st of October, 2005, the Prosecution would like to request to be admitted into evidence under the rule of 92 bis the following statements and transcripts. And there is just one remark here before I go into the list, so to say, is that when it comes to four witnesses, which I will mention by name, there are both statements, written statements and transcripts. For the rest of the witnesses that the Prosecution will request to be admitted under Rule 92(D), that is to say only the transcripts. And at last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you just pause while I check that we are in public session?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the last issue on this topic, that is I will address a witness, whose name is Mark Wheeler, but I take that to the last. So when it comes to, as said, written statements and some transcripts, when it comes to the witness Yvonne Milewski, bearing the e-court ID number 0294-7921, and that is a statement, 0294-7921. That is the e-court number. 2921. Yeah. And that is a statement on the 18th of June, 2003, and a following report about her findings at the autopsy of Ovcara examinations. And I have been told by the court officer that I don't need to call out the ERN number. That is correct. And further on, for the next witness, there is the witness Serge Krieger-Woinowsky, it's a written statement, and the e-court number is 0600-0053. And he was giving a statement on the 14th of November, 1997. Those two witnesses, both Milewski and Krieger, has given a specific certification under the rule of 92 bis as well. The following witness, Stipan Kraljevic, is both a written statement and transcript. The e-court ID number for the written statement is 0295-4950. That statement was given on the 8th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, I am not entirely clear. Are you at the moment tendering these?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: According to the decision of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I thought you were going on to make some explanation about these. But I anticipate now as you progress that you are actually tendering them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. We need then to go back to the first statement, which is that of Yvonne Milewski, and it will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 381, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And now we go to the second statement, that of Serge Krieger-Woinowsky.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be received with exhibit number 382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next -- you can carry on, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So the next witness with the name of Stipan Kraljevic, bearing e-court number for his statement given on the 8th of November, 1995, 0295-4950. And in addition to that, concerning this witness, also a transcript from his testimony in the Milosevic case on the 27th of August, 2003. The pages 25411 up until 25462. Bearing the e-court ID number 4666-4615. And I also requesting that to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Kraljevic statement will be received with exhibit number 383, while the Kraljevic testimony transcript will be received with exhibit number 384.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, my apologies. I need to do a correction here from my case manager. When it comes to the last witness transcript from the case of Milosevic, that is bearing e-court ID number IM00-4666. The rest is correct. It was only this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So continue to the next witness. That is Luka Sutalo. And he has -- which the Prosecution requests to be tendered into evidence. That is a statement given by this witness on the 17th April, 1999 with an additional addendum on the 18th of June, 2003. This statement is having the e-court ID number 0297-8997. And in addition to the written statement and the addendum, there is also transcript from the Milosevic case given on the 28th of August, 2003, with the pages 25540, 25587, bearing the ID court number IM00-4366. Regarding this witness, Luka Sutalo, and the previous one, Kraljevic, both of them have certifications, certifications under the Rule 92 bis, according to the Rules and Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber assumes, unless you indicate to the contrary, that each of the statements tendered are now in a form that complies with the Rule. So if there is any deficiency, we rely upon you to draw it our attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, you can do that correctly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Luka Sutalo statement will become Exhibit 385, while the Luka Sutalo testimony transcript will become exhibit number 386.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. The following witness with the name Pajo Nedic, and the e-court number IM00-4607, the Prosecution is requesting to be admitted into evidence only the transcript from his testimony in Dokmanovic case on the 26th of May, 1998. Page numbers 3135, 3160. The following witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With exhibit number 387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And then the following witness, that is Bogdan Vojnovic, e-court ID number IM00-46 -- 45, sorry, 4564, the Prosecution is requesting to have his transcript testimony in Dokmanovic case admitted into evidence, given on the 26th of May, 1998, bearing the pages 3160, 3196. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Vojnovic testimony will become 388.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The next witness is a protective measures witness, so that's where I will not mention the name but the number, pseudonym number, and that is P-028. E-court ID number is IM00-4520. Prosecution is here also requesting to be admitted into evidence transcript of his testimony given in the Dokmanovic case on the 28th of April, 1998. Pages 2579 up until 2554.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number 389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I have a correction to make, another one, actually. And that is the page number. I was mention here pages 2579 up until 2554. Correctly it should be 2479 up until 2554. Okay. And then we have -- let me see now, is there anything -- yeah. The last one, that is a witness with -- bearing the name of Ilja Koncarevic, e-court ID number IM00-4436. Also here, the Prosecution is requesting to have admitted into evidence the -- his testimony given in Dokmanovic trial, and accordingly the transcript given on the 25th of May, 1998, and the page numbers 3047, 30572 [sic]. It is 3047 up until 3072. So it's -- yeah, pages from 3047 to 3072. Yeah. That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That includes -- that will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Koncarevic transcript will become exhibit number 390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now that concludes the documents that you tender pursuant to Rule 92 bis and our earlier decision?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, Your Honours. But there is one specific issue left, actually. And that is regarding the witness Mark Wheeler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the Prosecution would like to ask the Defence team regarding the witness Mark Wheeler, if there is any attempt from the Defence side to have him cross-examined as an expert or to have agreed upon to have him admitted under the 92 bis and according to the decision of this Trial Chamber on the 21st of October, 2005, having in mind that the Defence, in the response to the Prosecution motion regarding the 92 bis material, raised a request to have Mark Wheeler cross-examined, and the Trial Chamber did not allow that in its decision on the 21st of October, 2005. So I would like to ask the Defence with the permittance of the Trial Chamber, of course, if the Defence would object for me to request this material to be admitted under 92 bis. If so, the Prosecution will today only request to put into evidence Mr. Wheeler's transcript from former evidence given to the -- in this Court. And we have been able to locate Mr. Wheeler, and he will be as soon as possible able to give us a certification, so his statement, written statement, or report, can be admitted then under the Rule 92(B). I would also before the Defence answering the question, to inform the Defence that the Prosecution has today received an positive answer from Mark Wheeler, the witness, that he will be able to be in this court for possible cross-examination between the 15th and 19th of May, if needed to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So what you wish to do, if the Defence agrees, would be to tender, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, only the transcript of the former evidence given by Dr. Wheeler in the Dokmanovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, for the proceedings to date. But also if the Defence agreed to having admitted into his evidence given, admitted into evidence so -- because we would like to have his certification in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mrs. Tuma, are you now moving to a statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: There is, when it comes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is previous evidence given in Dokmanovic. With respect to that, you want to know whether there is any objection to that being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yeah, when it comes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Quite separately, there is a statement given by Dr. Wheeler and you want to know whether it can be admitted subject to cross-examination, or what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The position from the Prosecution side is that we request to have -- first to have, if the Defence agree to that, to have Mark Wheeler admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis. Today the transcript and as soon as we have received his certification. But will be done between the 15th and 19th of May and then to have the -- his statement admitted into evidence after he's given his certification or declaration under Rule 92(B).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you are asking separately whether the Defence now will agree to his statement being received into evidence under Rule 92 bis as soon as the procedural formalities are concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic, can I start with you? First, with respect to the transcript of Dr. Wheeler from the Dokmanovic trial. Is there any issue about it being received today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the transcript from the Dokmanovic trial is concerned, it has always been our position that -- to ask to be given a chance to cross-examine this witness. We need to establish the time-frame and the context for this particular indictment. I have no objection to the transcript being admitted, but I stand by our previous request to be given a chance to cross-examine this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. -- Ms. Tapuskovic. Is your position the same as Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Miroslav Radic's Defence shares Mr. Vasic's position in relation to the transcript issue. In relation to the issue of Dr. Wheeler and his report, Miroslav Radic's Defence, under Rule 94 bis, has served on the Court a note informing the Court of our intention to cross-examine this witness. There was a Court ruling on the 21st of October, but that was only in relation to the Dokmanovic transcripts. Therefore, we stand by our previous position as expressed in our 94 bis motion. I might as well say something about the 92 bis admissions, because that's what the Defence teams have agreed amongst ourselves. We have no objections to any of the proposals just made by my learned friend. We have no objections to transcripts or to statements. We have all the documents for witness Milewski and for witness Krieger-Woinowsky. We have received 92 bis certificates, and these arrived in a timely manner. The same applies to Kraljevic, Stipan and Sutalo, Luka, who previously testified in the Milosevic case. Their statements were admitted at the time under 92 bis. Therefore, we have no objections to their transcripts from the Milosevic case or indeed their statements being admitted, except in relation to witness Wheeler under Rule 94 bis, as I've just specified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honours. I have nothing against the transcript being admitted under Rule 92 bis, but I hope that will in no way prejudice the privilege of the Defence to cross-examine on the statement only. If a ruling is made that the witness should appear and be cross-examined, I hope it won't be a problem confronting the witness with some of the facts that he mentioned in his testimony. I believe it would be more practical to have this admitted when the witness finally appears and when we start cross-examining Mr. Wheeler. I think in terms of purely practical aspects it would be better to do this once Mr. Wheeler is actually physically present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript of Dr. Wheeler in the Dokmanovic trial will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, the position of any further evidence of Dr. Wheeler, whether a statement or orally, can be dealt with when the witness is available. You may want to move under 89(F) for the statement; but the Defence, as we have indicated in our original decision, is not going to be denied an opportunity to cross-examine Dr. Wheeler.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will do nothing about any statement at the moment and that will be dealt with when you are ready with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That concludes your -- not quite, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Not quite, Your Honour. You can read me well, thank you for that. When it comes to exhibits regarding the transcripts that has been admitted into evidence today, I got a message last week from the court officer that we will, if so, by the end of business today to file a motion regarding the exhibits in the transcripts. If we decide from the Prosecution side to request them to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you did not move at the time of moving for the admission of the transcripts to have also admitted the exhibits that were tendered in the course of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No, because I got the message that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We look forward to your motion and see what should be made of it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I -- I have concluded this issue here when it comes to 92 bis. May I address the Trial Chamber in another -- just shortly, another topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And that is -- because tomorrow is my last day here in this Tribunal, and I would like to take the opportunity to express my gratitude to this Trial Chamber for me to be able to appear in front of you. It has been a great honour and a great pleasure for me to do that. I have learned a lot, and I will take that knowledge with me to my next position. And I also take the opportunity to say thank you for the whole Defence team. It has been a true pleasure and a good cooperation. And I wish you all, both the Prosecution team, Defence team, and also Your Honours, good luck with the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Tuma. And as we indicated on Friday, we wish you well in your new judicial role.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I am usually the one to have this pleasant duty to thank our learned friend on behalf of all three Defence teams. I wish to thank her for her cooperation and wish her every luck in her new position on behalf of all of our Defence teams. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. You are free to go about your new business, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: But before that, I will have a glass of champagne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it Mr. Smith who is carrying on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll be here for quite a while, so no farewells yet. Your Honour, we have a witness available this morning, he is a military witness, and we have binders which have been distributed and Your Honours may have it. So we can proceed with him now; we just need to logistically swap over. And the witness is Mr. Trifunovic. Your Honour, before the witness enters, perhaps if I just mention the folder that is being distributed that would relate to this particular witness. It contains 37 documents or parts of documents which are both in English and B/C/S. I believe Your Honours may have received these folders already. This folder relates to some rules and regulations relating to the JNA, et cetera. And largely it relates to documents that were made and reports that were made during the time of the Vukovar operation from the guards brigade. These documents have been disclosed to the Defence. Most of them are Rule 65 ter numbers, but for the ones are not, which is probably about seven or eight, they were discovered after the filing of the exhibit or the exhibit list -- in terms of discovered, I mean received by the Prosecution. And they have been given to the Defence well in advance. I believe they have copies of the hard folder, as well as they have received a list of the particular documents that we are to use today. But perhaps I'll say a bit more about it after the witness is sworn in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's being prepared, could I indicate for all counsel that in the days when we sit from 9.30 to 4.30. We will break between approximately 12.30 and 1.30 for lunch. And we will have a -- in the absence of redactions, a 20-minute break between about 10 minutes to 11.00 and 10 past 11.00. All of these times, of course, are subject to precisely where a witness is in evidence and as you realise, we are a little flexible about times. And in the afternoon, similarly, midway between 1.30 and 4.30 there will be a 20-minute break somewhere at approximately that time. Good morning, sir. Would you please take the card that is shown to you and read aloud the affirmation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you state your full name to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Radoje Trifunovic, son of Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And your age, I believe you are currently retired, and your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am 54 years old, and I am a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the last position you held or the last job you had before you commenced retirement?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The last duty I performed before I retired was deputy commander of the guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe you retired about a month ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on April 1st of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This probably isn't how you planned to spend your retirement, but we appreciate your presence in the courtroom. Is it correct that the Prosecution has obviously requested you to come here to provide evidence at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it also correct that prior to coming here that you have spoken to at least one of the Defence lawyers in relation to this case, on numerous occasions?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can go to your military training and education. You said that you were the deputy commander of the guards brigade, and I believe this is the guards brigade that was based in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you join the JNA, approximately what year?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the JNA in 1977, after having completed my studies at the military academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long were your studies for when you first began in the JNA, your initial studies?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Four years, initially, at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was this at the reserve officers' school?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, at the military academy for land forces in Belgrade. The reserve officers' school is the first post I had after completion of military academy from 1977 until 1981. This was in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: During that four years at the military academy, briefly can you explain the types of subjects that you studied, in a very brief form?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the subjects, expert subjects, were of a military nature. As far as general education goes, there were many subjects from civilian universities such as mathematics, chemistry, philosophy, psychology and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then after you finished at the military academy, what position did you hold, and what duties did you have?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was the reserve officers' school in Bileca, I was the commander of the cadets platoon from 1977 until 1981. This was for four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 1981 were you transferred to Derventa, to a JNA motorised battalion there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1981, and I stayed there until 1989, in Derventa, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what positions or what ranks did you hold during that eight-year period?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In 1981, I was captain; in 1989, I was captain first class. This was towards the end, because in 1990 I was granted the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what command positions did you hold during that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Platoon commander in Bileca, this was a cadet's platoon; this is the lowest functional post. In Derventa, in 1981, I assumed the command of a company for two or three years, then I was deputy commander of a motorised battalion and battalion commander until 1989 until I was sent for continued training and education once again in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you do that training and education, what type of school was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This was the command staff academy at the time in Belgrade. And it was a two-year period of training for the level of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you studied -- you testified that you studied for about four years when you commenced in the JNA. Can you tell us what type of studies were involved in this two-year period? How were they different?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a higher degree education for duties of commander of a brigade. So it's still at the tactical level. Duties of a brigade commander and duties in higher command staffs were dealt with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say these studies were at a tactical level, what do you mean by "tactical level"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The tactical level is up to the level of a brigade. All the levels above the brigade are operational or operative; there is also a strategic level. So this particular training implied training for command duties at the tactical level and duties of staff officers in operations commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 1991 did you join the guards brigade then?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was on the 15th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the full name of the guards brigade is, the formal name?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know it changed, but specifically at the time that I arrived, it was called the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what position did you have there and what rank did you have when you started in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was the senior staff officer at the operations and training body and the Guards Motorised Brigade headquarters or staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly can you explain what a senior staff officer does?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: These duties are regulated for any staff officer in the operations organ. Amongst them the senior staff officer duties are to participate in proposals, planning and command work in adopting various decisions, the drafting of plans, which is part of the planning function, orders certain assessments and calculations. But this was not specifically laid down, so that some of these functions that are mentioned in some segments were in the jurisdiction of other staff officers in the operations and training organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say in that role that you were a direct assistant, high-level assistant to the commander of the brigade? Is that reasonable?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As a staff officer, no. But as chief of the operations organ I believe, and it is certainly a duty of a high-level assistant to the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You referred to the functions of the staff officer. Did the functions change between peacetime activities and wartime activities, and if it did, can you tell the main difference and the change, say wartime activities generally?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There are no significant differences. The wartime situation itself and the form of the planning and the entire documentation that had to be implemented makes it essential for work to be carried out more specifically and more quickly in quite specific conditions. What is done in peacetime is done in wartime, but of course one has to adapt to the wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Much of your evidence today will be about the topic of the guards brigade involvement in the Vukovar operation. Is it correct that you went to Vukovar and you were there for the period of September, 30th of September to the 24th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps just to finish off your education and experience in the military, when you arrived back from Vukovar, what position did you take up and how long did you hold that for until there was a change?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: On my return from Vukovar I continued to perform the duties of senior staff officer until November, 1992, when I was appointed chief of the organ or sector for operations and training. I continued to perform this function until May, 1994, when I was appointed as assistant for logistics. Now this is -- title has changed, the title of assistant for logistics. I spent a full 10 years in this post, until 2004 when, sometime in mid-June, I was appointed as deputy commander of what is now the guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then from June 2004 until April 2006, you held this position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the last rank that you held before you retired from the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in 2002 did you attend the General Staff school?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 2002 I completed the General Staff school, that's the highest level of education in the armed forces, and this took one year. I did not hand over my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You've testified that you've done quite a bit of study in the military to get to the position that you ended up with. This period of study at the General Staff school, this period of time, what type of study was that? What was different to it compared to the other that you had done?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is training for the highest levels of command, or for other duties at highest commands of operations and strategic levels, meaning that when we're talking about command, this is up to corps commander and above, when we're talking about staff duties in operation commands corps, armies, although at the time that I went through my training there were no armies. So we're talking about the most responsible functions in the operations sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question before the break: How long was the training at the General Staff school?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The last one in the General Staff school, that took a year. The one before that took two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've finished that topic, so it may be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. We will now have a 20-minute break and resume at 10 past 11.00. And for that purpose we will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, briefly before I question the witness further, I earlier talked about the binder and its make-up, et cetera. But just briefly. In relation to the binder there's 37 tabs, there is an index at the front. The index at the front states the 65 ter number, the date of the document, the description, and the English ERN and the B/C/S ERN. Now, these documents are in e-court, but as Your Honour has suggested, a hard copy version perhaps sometimes can make things run as smoothly as possible. In relation to the documents, especially documents number 1 -- 1 to 7, which are laws, regulations and principles from manuals in the -- in the JNA, they have only been included in part, relating to the relevant sections that we would like the witness to focus on. However, there are other aspects of those manuals, et cetera, which we will be relying on, but it's not required that the witness goes through that today. Behind each tab we have the English version first and then we have the B/C/S version. The witness has a copy of this folder, an exact reproduction of what we have. And in a number of cases, especially in relation to the regulations and laws, et cetera, we've put some introductory pages to show the title of the document, just for authentification purposes, and the relevant provision will sort of follow after that. But hopefully it will go as smoothly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before we had break we talked about the education and training that you'd had with the JNA since 1977. Now I would like to discuss some of the laws, some of the regulations, some of the principles that were incorporated into the JNA and also enacted by law in the former Yugoslavia back in 1991, or were applicable in 1991. What I would like to do is ask you a few questions that will help the Trial Chamber and all parties understand some aspects of the structure of the JNA and the armed forces and some of the principles relating to combat operations, such as command and control, and areas of responsibility and forces, et cetera. Perhaps if we can start at the beginning with number 1, tab number 1. This document is from the socialist former Republic of -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it's a law relating to the All People's Defence, and it was issued in 1982. The ERN number, English, is 0046-1889 to 0046-1924; and the B/C/S ERN is 0216-6067 to 0216-6102. And it's 65 ter number 387. Witness, can you -- do you have that document in front of you now with the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that document, and were you familiar with it in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just briefly, can you explain the purpose of the -- of the Law on All People's Defence and the basic principle which underpinned it, just briefly what the law is about, and then I'll ask you some questions about some specific provisions. In your own words.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on All People's Defence is one of the laws adopted by the federal assembly. Specifically, the Law on All People's Defence covers the organisation of all matters pertaining to the defence of the country regulating the main rights and duties of all the people and citizens, basic and other organisation of associated labour, according -- relating to all matters of defence of the country, and established by the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as well as basic rights and duties of all parties in the state system that are part the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps if you can look at Article 91, where it talks about what the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of what they comprised of. Do you have Article 91 in front of you, page 61 of the English?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you read that article to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Article 91: "The armed forces make up a single entity and are comprised of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. "Any citizen who with weapons, or in any other fashion, participates in the resistance against the enemy is also considered a member of the armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the international laws of war that apply to the armed forces in combat operation, if we look at Article 93, can you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Article 93: "During combat activities, members of the armed forces are obliged at all times and in all circumstances to abide by the rules of the international law of war on the humane treatment of wounded and captured enemies, on the protection of the civilian population and other regulations in this law, in compliance with the Constitution and the law."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Further in the article it describes in more detail what Territorial Defence means in the armed forces. And that can be found at Article 102. Can you look at that provision and tell me whether you are familiar with it, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can read that article, then I will just ask you a couple of questions about it. But don't read the full article, please. Perhaps the first three paragraphs, and then I'll tell you to stop, and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Territorial Defence shall be the broadest aspect of an organised grassroots resistance. "Territorial Defence shall be organised in basic and other organisations of associated labour, at the level of local communes, municipalities, autonomous provinces, republics and other socio-political communities. "Territorial Defence shall comprise all armed formations which are not incorporated in the Yugoslav People's Army and the police. "Territorial Defence shall comprise units, institutions and staffs, and other forms of organisations of working people and citizens for a general popular armed resistant. "Territorial Defence units and institutions, and other forms of organisations of working people and citizens for a general popular armed resistance shall be set up and trained in peacetime and engaged in wartime in the event of an immediate threat of war or in other emergencies as well as during exercises, ... and in the course of other assignments in time of peace envisaged by this Law."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can stop you there, you referred to in that article that: "The Territorial Defence shall comprise of all armed formations which are not incorporated in the Yugoslav People's Army ..." Did -- in your experience, did that happen in practice?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can move to Article 103, briefly can you say what the article states in relation to command and control, the principle of command and control and how it applies to the Territorial Defence and explain that a little, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Article 103?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Territorial Defence shall be organised and set up within a joint system of all-people's defence, in accordance with the Constitution, law fundamentals of organisation and outlines of plans of development of the armed forces and a plan of their use, the system of command and control in the armed forces, a common system of arms procurement, equipment and training of the armed forces and the decisions and plans of socio-political communities." You wanted to have my comment, I presume. The Territorial Defence is organised up to the level of republic of a given republic inside the country. And the highest command levels are the organs of a given republic. As one goes down towards municipalities and local communes and other organisations of associated labour, the commanding of the Territorial Defence falls under their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move to Article 119 and this article relates to volunteers. And perhaps if I read the section that is contained in that, and then I will ask you to comment, please. In Article 119, the second paragraph found in English states: "In times of war, in the event of an immediate threat of war or in other emergencies the armed forces may also be reinforced with volunteers. "Volunteers as referred to in this Article, are considered to be persons not subject to military service and who have been accepted in joined the armed forces at their own request." And then the last paragraph in the English version it states that: "Persons referred to in paragraphs 2 and 4 of this Article shall have the same rights and duties as military personnel and/or military conscripts." Do you see that part of the article of 119?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In -- in 1991 in Vukovar were volunteers made part of the armed forces? We'll discuss in more detail later, but just a simple yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as I said earlier, at the moment we're just discussing the regulations and laws and principles that applied in 1991, and we'll discuss what happened in Vukovar shortly. And if you can look at Article 112, please. And this relates to principles of command and control. If you can read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Command in the armed forces shall be founded on the principles of unity of command with respect to the use of forces and resources, unity of authority and the obligation to implement decisions, commands and orders of a superior officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when it mentions the principles of unity of command, what does that mean? In general terms at the moment.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The armed forces are comprised of two elements: The JNA and the Territorial Defence. The command of either of the elements needs to be unified from top to bottom. In this case, in the way I interpret this article, that means that the command of the JNA and the TO should be organised from the top, from the highest level, being the Supreme Defence Council at the time; that is, the body under whose jurisdiction the command of the armed forces was. Because both of the elements are subordinated to that highest instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that unity of command, how does that relate to how authority or power is exercised, if you can explain further.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In order to command in a unified fashion and from one single level, irrespective of what level within the system we are talking about, it has to be carried out by one single person, one commander. That, in brief, is the principle of singleness of command, the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, if we look at Article 107, and if you can indicate who, in fact, is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, or who was, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then if we look at Article 108, it mentions about the president being able to transfer powers, and to who. Can you describe a bit further, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: One of the tasks of the president of the then SFRY was to organise the country's defence system. Having in mind all of the other authority vested in him and having in mind the level of expert knowledge of this organ, being the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, it was logical to be able to transfer certain of its duties in the sphere of command and control to the Federal Secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can move to Article 110, it talks a little more about the federal secretary of national defence. If you can read that out, please, and then I'll ask you some questions about that section.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Article 110: "The Federal Secretary for National Defence shall exercise the duties of command and control of the armed forces in keeping with the powers transferred to him, pursuant to the SFRY Constitution, by the SFRY Presidency, and in keeping with the federal law. "The chief of the General Staff shall replace the federal secretary for the national defence in the event of the latter's absence or inability to discharge the duties referred to in paragraph 1 of the Article. "Commanders of units and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army shall carry out the command and control duties of the Yugoslav People's Army in accordance with the federal law."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At -- in 1991, who was the federal secretary of national defence, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I remember. That was General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the chief of the General Staff of the federal secretary, do you know who he was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do. It was General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. When, to the best of your knowledge, in 1991 was this law in operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be precise. As regards the events in 1991 and onwards, it was a difficult situation in which one would have to pass new laws. Perhaps there were some amendments to the law, but I believe this was the form of the law that stood at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now move to tab 2, please. This is 65 ter number 383. It relates -- a segment of the manual for work of commands and staff dated 1983. The ERN number is K011 to 1600 to K011 to 1794; B/C/S is K0239361 to K0239576. Colonel, have you seen this document before, before coming to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain what the purpose of this document is? You only have a part of the document there, but the purpose of the manual? In general terms.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The work of commands and staffs is a serious matter. One which demands precise regulation. The previous manual on the work of commands and staffs became obsolete. This particular draft was the result of new ideas and work as regards the functioning of commands and staffs, in peacetime as well as in times of war. It also contains additional issues that is needed to be regulated and harmonised with the Law on All People's Defence that we have discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we look at Article 358, or paragraph 358, which, in the English is written as 385, but that's a translation error, it discusses the role of the command in an attack operation. And at one point it states: "The commander must at all times know the status, position and capabilities of his units two levels down." In the context of that article, can you give some explanation as to what that means?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As stated, any given command needs to monitor the situation constantly in order to be informed about the situation on the ground, and that information had to be forwarded to the commander so that he could appropriately assess the situation and issue decisions, as well as correct them, if needed. In order to have a true reflection of the situation, reports and the situation, the reports must be sent as well as the situation followed from the lowest, from the grassroot levels all the way up to the commander. By being informed of the situation two levels down, the given commander can react properly by issuing decisions or correcting his own previous decision. And, as far as I know, one can read this in all military manuals preceding this draft and even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that the reports must be sent as well as the situation from the lowest -- the grassroot level, all the way up to the commander, what are the basic levels of command in a normal military structure? I'm talking about companies and brigades, et cetera. What would be the grassroot level, and then what would be the highest level, if you can explain?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The grassroot, or the lowest level of command, is a squad, by squad leaders. And they send oral reports to their platoon commanders. Platoon commanders, in turn, in an oral or written form, informs -- inform company commanders. Orally it's usually done during briefings, and if need be, they can send written reports. Company commanders report to battalion commanders usually in a written form or via communications, or in briefings. Battalion commanders inform brigade commanders written -- by written orders or via communications or orally. It can be done directly with the commander or in the presence of other officers of the staff or command during briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You talk about each level having a responsibility to -- to report, either oral or in written form, matters. What about the commander's responsibility to seek that information, if reports are not coming? Is there any responsibility for a commander to do that, in light of what's written in this section?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to a decision being made to undertake a certain activity or when a written decision needs to be corrected, in each such document the commander needs to specify that he wants reports to be submitted from all levels reflecting the situation at a given point of time and specifying the dead-line for the submission of such reports. This is what is asked for by the commander. Then, by a commander's decision, he can also request oral reports concerning some information that he believes he should know or receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the specific wording of the section, it says: "The commander must at all times know the status, position and capabilities of units two levels down." When you read those words, "Must at all times know," does that relate to any duty on the commander, and how would that duty be carried out, if it does?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I have explained how he should receive information. He needs to have information from all levels in order to be able to control, and that duty is personally bestowed upon him, or perhaps such a duty can be carried out by other officers as well, together with the commander. All the reports that reflect the situation on the ground provide the commander with such information that at any given point in time he can assess the situation in any given unit properly. Of course we are not discussing here the accuracy of those reports. If one submits a report that is incorrect, that person can be instituted proceedings against, or disciplined. Personal knowledge of the commander is an important element of control, and a clearly established command system needs to be set up through precise and timely reporting, resulting in accurate and timely information at the disposal of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to summarise, is this duty, would you say it was an active duty on the commander to seek this information, or a passive duty, just to receive it? What does the duty imply?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It encompasses the obligation of all to report accurately and reliably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does it encompass the obligation of the commander to seek out information, if those reports are not forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes reports are not forwarded, but it is a duty of the commander to ask for such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we look at the title of the section, it states: "The work of the command during an attack." Would this, shall we say, situational awareness of units two levels down, this duty, would that also apply in post-attack and pre-attack situations, or are we just talking about the attack itself? In principle, I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In all situations. Of course, before the attack one has a more realistic picture and the situation is known. The commander is supposed to follow the situation. During the activities themselves, he also needs to monitor. That is at any given point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I was remiss, I didn't tender the first document. I seek to tender at tab number 1, which is 65 ter 387, the Law on All People's Defence, and I also seek to tender tab number 2, 65 ter 383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First of all, tab 1, the extracts from the Law on All People's Defence, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then tab 2, the extracts from the manual on the work of commands and staffs will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 393, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour, the Prosecution will be seeking to tender the full document, which has been disclosed to the Defence, and is in e-court, but for the purpose of the hearing today, we are just highlighting a couple of aspects of it, but we believe it to be relevant, the full document, both full documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if you can turn to tab 3, please. This is 65 ter number 384. And it's the JNA -- excerpts from the JNA text-book on command and control dated 1983 and it relates to chapter 1, the functions of command and control. And the English ERN is L006-3323 to L006-3474; and the B/C/S ERN 0214-8123 to 0214-8517. Witness, do you see the excerpt from the JNA text-book on command and control in your binder?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just in your own words, can you explain what the purpose and the content of this JNA text-book on command and control is? Just briefly, and then we'll look at some particular sections. What does the manual attempt to do?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Command and control constitute the most important segment within the system of armed combat. A theoretical knowledge of the principles of command and control, as well as the application of these principles in practice, guarantee organised adherence to these principles, encompassing also control and coordination. There must be a guarantee that these will be implemented in an organised way and that the objective of armed combat will be achieved, as defined. This is a document that outlines a system governing organisation at all -- of command at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at part 6 of the manual, which is page 35 in English, it's entitled "Functions of command and control." If you can read that introductory paragraph, then I might ask you a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Functioning of command and control. In order to attain a goal, which in this case means generally effective command and control, several correlated operations need to be performed. These essential and linked operations are named the functions of command and control. These are mutually dependent, interrelated, and conditioned. These functions encompass the entire process of command and control from the beginning to the end - see figure 2. There are no discernible lines of division between the functions because their implementation depends on interaction. The command and control process consists of the following functions: Planning, organising, command, coordination (concerted action) and control (figure 2)."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can just ask you a question about how organisation is a function of command and control, if you move to the section that states -- that's entitled "Figure 2, organisation." And then in the English on page 43, and I think it might be three paragraphs down in the B/C/S, I'll read out to you what it says about organisation and I'll ask you to comment. "An effective organisation helps the performers of a combat mission (commands,, commanders and commanding officers) to get a clear notion of the set goal. The tasks stem from a goal; hey must be realistic and assigned to specific participants (performers), and limited in time and space (beginning and end). The command and control organs must be familiar with and follow the situation in units, which can be ensured through organising a system of reporting and supervising the progress of all missions." I'm not sure whether you found that section, but did you hear what I just read out to you from that -- from that manual?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I heard it from you, but what my tab says is organising or organisation at item 2. Not organisation, but rather "organising." But organisation is not one of the functions listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. That may have been my error. It may be an error in the translation, so thank you for clarifying that. But particularly in that section, further down, it states that: "Command and control can be ensured through organising a system of reporting and supervising the progress of all missions." Can you explain how that should be implemented? Sorry, I can't assist you with -- it's -- the section should be about 20 lines down, and it starts out with "an effective organisation." Perhaps if you --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Organising." The essence of organising as a function of command and control is to secure a solution for the implementation of a decision in terms of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a process of establishing the entire system to be used to -- for the implementation of a task. Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's not. If you move further down and turn over the page, please. It's the paragraph that's just before the list of the principles that are part of the function of organising. It's the paragraph just before that. And there's a sentence in the -- at the end of the paragraph that says: "The command and control organs must be familiar with and follow the situations in units, which can be ensured through organising a system of reporting and supervising the progress of all missions."

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend, but I think it might be a good idea to read out to the witness a passage as a whole in relation to a given subject. This is taking usually a single sentence out of its natural context, which may leave the witness nonplused, so my objection is more about a matter of principle than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic, but I don't think that is a particular problem with this witness who clearly knows the subject, and he will be able to fill in a context, if that is necessary. Carry on, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you comment on that duty to ensure an organised system of reporting and supervising the progress of all missions and what that should entail in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms this means that the organs of command must monitor situations, and based on their monitoring activity they must be familiar with situations. This can be ensured by organising the reporting system and by double-checking any missions being accomplished. In order to gain an insight into a situation and in order to be able to make an informed decision, one must have an accurate report. One must check whether all the tasks are being carried out in keeping with the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is what is generally implied by control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the command and control process, this manual states that control is also a function of this command and control, and in the English translation on page 48 the heading is entitled, number 5, "Inspection." Do you see that section further down where it talks about an inspection or control in heading 5? It's English page 48.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can ask you to read, say, the first 10 or so lines of that, I'll tell you when to stop, and then if you can comment on how that would be implemented, that inspection or control.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Inspection is a function of command and control, which provides an insight into the status and degree of accomplishment of the assigned tasks. It is organised and conducted incessantly in the course of all other functions. Through inspection comparison is made between the planned or anticipated results and those actually achieved over a specific time-frame. Negative phenomena and their causes are detected through an analysis of results. Only then is it possible to take appropriate measures conducive to a successful completion of tasks and generally achieving better results. However, inspection must not" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can stop you there, sorry for interrupting, but if we can move further down the section, and it's just above the part where it states: "The effectuation of inspection as an organisation feature is based on the following principles." And then it lists subsection 1. Above that section there is a sentence that says: "The role of inspection should be seen as a standing obligation and duty, it must not be arbitrary, but rather based on science and the established system of norms and criteria." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain in practical terms what it means by this -- "this role of inspection should be based on science and the establishment of systems and norms"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you ask me, the role of inspection is paramount, second only to the role of command. Inspection is used to define and assess what the real situation is. Based on science or on scientific principles, as well as this reference to criteria means, in my opinion, that no inspection within the JNA can be disorganised, no inspection must display a lack of planning or a lack of objective. No inspection in the JNA must fail to show the situation as it is. That is why inspection is organised in several different ways. One way is control exercised -- inspection carried out personally by the commander.
