Another way would be to send teams, command teams out with specific tasks, having previously studied all the principles, regulations, rules and decisions made by the commander in order to ensure an appropriate reaction and appropriate monitoring. So these are the norms and criteria governing inspection. Of course, there are always several ways to conduct an activity, and each and every activity is governed by its own criteria. The important thing is to have these criteria incorporated into an overall inspection plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. One -- one facet of -- or one function of command and control that is mentioned in this manual is coordination. But there is a section relating to coordination explaining what it means. But rather than perhaps going through the text of it, could you explain to the Court how coordination is a function of command and control and why -- and why it's important?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The same thing applies to any type of activity. In the military, coordination is of paramount importance. Coordination is used to harmonise a wide range of issues from a wide range of different areas, from the sphere of economics, from the sphere of production, the use and coordination of units in a combat area, cooperation with socio-political organisations and communities, in the sense of contributing to the accomplishment of an assigned task. Coordination actually means coordinated action. When there is no coordinated action, when there is no coordinated action that is fully implemented, not only can there be no results, but one can also incur great and significant losses to one's own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But just very briefly, in your own words, as an experienced commander, why is coordination so important in a combat operation, the coordinating of different units? Just very succinctly, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Very succinctly. Coordination means coordinated action between all those involved in combat activities while accomplishing a given mission. Why is it important? It is used to coordinate all activities in geographical terms, in terms of the time-frame and in terms of the main agents. If there is no coordination, combat activity would be erratic or chaotic and the possibility of undesired effects would be great.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender the JNA text-book on command and control, which is tab number 3, and 65 ter number 384.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 394.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can move to the JNA brigade rules for infantry, motorised, mountain, alpine, and marine and light brigades issued by the Federal Secretariat of the People's Defence in 1984, in tab number 4. And the ERN number is -- the English 0303-0230 to 0303-0415; and the B/C/S is 0114-7096 to 0114-7391. Witness, do you have the brigade rules in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you explain what brigade rules, what the purpose and content of the brigade rules are? Just in your own words, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As all rules, the brigade rules constitute a manual that is used to tackle issues of control and command exercised over units. The brigade rules apply to the brigade level, to the level of a brigade commander. They encompass all issues related to the use and principles of use of brigades, both in peacetime and during war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can look at paragraph 12 which is, on the English, page 6, and the heading is: "Assignment, zone of operation and grouping of forces." Do you see paragraph 12 there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In this paragraph it talks about the assignment that the brigade shall -- the brigade will receive in combat operations. Can you briefly read out the first two paragraphs of Article 12 or paragraph 12, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 12: "A brigade shall receive its combat assignments from its superior command. Whenever possible, the superior command may also regulate the manner in which the assignment is to be carried out. "When a brigade does not receive an assignment from its superior command, the commander of the brigade shall give an assignment on his own initiative according to the general concept and situation. "The basic task of a brigade is to carry out continual and varied combat operations and to inflict on the enemy as many casualties and as much damage to its combat vehicles and other equipment as possible, to break up and exhaust its forces, and to gain and hold territory in a given zone. "A task is carried out gradually" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, if you can just stop there, thank you. In that section it explains the basic task of a brigade and then it states that one of the tasks is to gain and hold territory in a given zone. In we look at paragraph 13, this relates to zone of operations. And if you can briefly read this paragraph out and then I'll ask you a few questions about it. And if -- I know it's time consuming, but if you could read a little more slowly, just for the translators that are translating your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "A brigade shall be assigned a zone of operations in which to carry out its tasks (zone of attack, zone of defence, zone of march and suchlike). Depending on the tasks, mainly in temporarily occupied territory, a brigade may be assigned an area of combat operations. "Zone of operations is a territory of limited width and depth in which a brigade organises and carries out combat operations. Its size depends on: The type of brigade, the features of the terrain, the task, the brigade's place and role in the combat position within the higher unit, its condition and combat capacities, strengthening strength of the TO units in the area, its support and suchlike. "In the assigned zone of action, the brigade's commander, in cooperation with all the different players involved in armed combat, organises systems of combat integrated in terms of goal, place and time. "An area of operations is a free territory within the temporarily occupied territory, usually in the operational or strategic depth, which has been assigned to the brigade for the purpose of implementing its tasks. In the area of operations, the commander of the brigade normally organises on his own initiative the carrying out of various combat operations and other activities according to the task assigned and the specific circumstances. "The brigade shall not or must not leave its assigned zone of operations or area without the approval of the commanding officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a difference between a zone of operations and a zone of responsibility, command responsibility, or would that be the same thing?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: A zone of operations is the same thing as a zone of responsibility, in terms of area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if a brigade commander was placed in command of a zone of operations, what would that mean in relation to other units operating in that zone of operations in terms of subordination, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean something in terms of executing combat assignments. All units within the assigned zone of operations would be affected and would fall under the unified system of command. What this means in practical terms is that a single commander is in charge of all the units within a given zone of operations. Whichever commander has been assigned by the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now move to the command provisions, chapter IV of the brigade rules, where it refers to a joint -- the joint provisions, and it's paragraph 107. And in the brigade rules it gives a definition of command of the brigade. But perhaps, before we move to that topic, I think it's time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing in the transcript, page 48, line 17, it reads Exhibit 384, whereas what it should read is Exhibit 394. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We will adjourn now for lunch, resuming at 12:00 -- at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we talked about some of the provisions of the brigade rules that applied were enacted in 1984 in relation to zones of operations and areas of operations. In your binder, this is in tab 4, you'll see some brigade rules that specifically talk about command and control issues at the brigade level. It's English page 35, it's chapter IV, "command," and it has "joint provisions." And it starts with paragraph 107. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to read out the first paragraph then ask you some questions about the terms that are used. Paragraph 107 states: "Command of the brigade is part of an integrated system of command and control which is based on adopted principles of command. Command implies the best ways of using human skills and the capabilities of equipment for the brigade to achieve the best possible results in performing a given task. To this end, command must be integrated, continuous, secure, flexible, effective and operational." I would like you to have a look at paragraph 108 in relation to integration as part of a command function. And if you can read that paragraph out, and then I want to ask you some questions about it, please. This is paragraph 108.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Integration of command is reflected in the directing of all units of the brigade and other subjects in its zone of combat actions towards a common objective. This is achieved through joint efforts of the brigade command and commands of the brigade's subordinate and other units and staff of the TO operating in coordination with the brigade, as well as in cooperation with the organisations and organs of DPZs, DPOs and OURs. "Integration is achieved by linking and coordinating the efforts of the brigade command with other organs of command on the basis of unity of command and subordination. To achieve integration of command it is necessary to organise an integrated system of communications and crypto-protection for all forces in the brigade's zone of operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to this principle of integration, what is your understanding of that section? Your understanding as a commander.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Unity of command implies commanding by one senior officer, one commander in the entire zone for the purposes of implementing a specific objective. That means that with this principle command, or one commander is superior and all the subjects in the area of responsibility or in the area of combat are subordinated to that one commander. In order to achieve this, full responsibility is required, as well as the investment of efforts by all for the resolution of all problems that are connected to the implementation of a particular objective. Coordinated action by TO units, cooperation with socio-political organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in this provision it states that command should be continuous. And if you can briefly read out the first sentence in paragraph 109 about this aspect of continuous, continuity, then can you tell -- tell the Court what your understanding is of that principle?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There should be no breaks in the continuity of command in order to achieve its continuous functioning and implementation of cooperation in joint action by all those indicating this process. Any break in the continuity of command would be an impediment in the implementation of objectives, which means all subordinate commanders are duty-bound to work towards the implementation of decisions in accordance to the tasks assigned to them in that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does this -- does this section relate to continuity of command in terms of time as well or not? And the frequency of that --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In terms of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The section also states that the command in a brigade must be flexible, and if we look at paragraph 111, I would ask that you briefly read that paragraph out, and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Flexibility of command means that the brigade command and commands of subordinate units can adapt rapidly to changes in the situation. An important pre-condition for flexibility is the degree to which commanding officers are trained to independently, on their own initiative and rapidly evaluate situations and solve complex combat problems in various conditions. "Flexibility of command is reflected in: The deployment, grouping of brigade units and other forces in its zone, which is most suitable in a given situation; the ability to rapidly transfer the emphasis of actions; the ability for rapid integration of actions by all forces in the zone of actions; and the ability to carry out combat actions in conditions of temporarily captured territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What is your view of the importance of this principle of flexibility in a brigade command? How important is it in exercising command in a brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's very important. Because changes in the situation are certain in the course of combat operations, and this is something that happens frequently. It implies the commander's skill, as well as the skill of subordinate commanders, to independently and on their own initiative, but in the spirit of the commander's decision, quickly evaluate the situation and solve the problems that crop up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Command in a brigade is stated that it also should be effective and operational. Can you read paragraph -- the first paragraph of 112, then I'll ask you to comment on it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Effectiveness and operativeness of command implies that the brigade command is capable of taking timely and correct decisions, communicate them quickly to subordinates, and, through them, of exerting effective influence over the implementation of that decision. "For the command to be effective and operational, the brigade command and commanding officers must be familiar with modern means of combat and their impact on the character of combat operations, and the characteristics of the terrain in the brigade's zone of operations." Ability to use units of the TO organisation of the organisations of associated labour and other organs and this requires a high level of ability of the command to continuously monitor the situation, take decisions and communicate them to subordinates. "The timely adoption of decisions, their rapid conveying to those charged with implementing them, and especially the results of operations are the basic measure of effective and operative command. A decision taken on time, even if it lacks some elements, is better and more effective than one that is taken with delay. "Initiative and courageous acceptance of responsibility, especially in complex situations, are another necessary condition for effective command."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can ask you to look at the section number 2 in relation to brigade command, this is paragraph 114. Can you -- can you read --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- that section out, please? And then explain what it means?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "The brigade command (scheme 2) is an organisational and establishment organ of the brigade whose role is to command and control the brigade. The brigade command should be equipped and trained to effectively integrate actions by all forces in the brigade's zone of deployment. "The organisational structure of the command depends on the type of brigade, its composition and the work it performs within its area of competence. It is also regulated and determined by the formation. "The activities" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How does a brigade commander effectively integrate actions by all forces in its zone, in its brigade zone? How would that be done, just in brief terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander unifies the actions of all the forces in the brigade's zone of operation. The decision he has made on the basis of proposals by all of the command organs that are illustrated on the chart, and once he has made the decision and specified the assignments of all the subordinate units, in one item of the decision he has specified also the tasks of the units which are in the area and which are not in the establishment of the brigade, which are resubordinated, actually, to the brigade. His decision also regulates the coordinated action on the basis of the decisions in the order of the superior command, some structures of the socio-political organisations and socio-political communities in his area of responsibility. Joint action is also regulated in a decision based on a decision or order by the superior command, which regulates that section of coordinated action in terms of coordinated action for the unit under command. So it practically unifies everything in his establishment composition and unifies everything that he has been tasked with in a decision or order by his superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at paragraph 115, it talks about the exclusive right of the brigade commander to command all brigade units and attached units. It states: "He bears full responsibility for the work of the brigade, command and subordinate structures and subordinate commands for the state of morale, for security and combat readiness, for training and for the proper performance of tasks." Then states: "The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their fulfillment, and demands their strict execution regardless of difficulties that arise." What is your understanding of this particular section?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: Just as in the previous articles of the rules in the theoretical part of the rules and regulations, the command function is indivisible. The commander makes a decision, sets the assignments, carries out inspection, and bears full responsibility for the work of the command of the brigade and for the work of the subordinate commands. And naturally he bears responsibility for the overall situation, here we're talking about morale, political state, state of training and readiness, combat readiness and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to paragraph 116, refers to the Chief of Staff of the brigade. What -- what is the function of the Chief of Staff of the brigade? What duties does he or she have?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: First the staff, it's the main organ or the basic organ in the command of the brigade. Functionally it links all the other organs of the brigade and integrates or unifies their tasks. He has the right of issuing orders in accordance with the commander's decision relating to the tasks these organisational units carry out in the staff. This is carried out or implemented by the Chief of Staff, and he is the only one who has the right to set assignments, but exclusively in line with the decision by the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And when -- sorry, continue.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: He is also a superior to the organ for operations and training, as well as all other organs. I was also a part of that organ, so I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were in Vukovar who was the Chief of Staff of the guards brigade; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of the guards brigade was Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we move to paragraph 146, please. This paragraph relates to how decisions are conveyed to subordinates. Can you read that paragraph and then I'll ask you a few questions about it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Conveying the decision to subordinates can be done orally or in writing, in the form of a command or an order. Regardless of whether it is issued from the command post of the brigade commander or during commander reconnaissance, a command is formulated as a written document. More important orders are formulated as written documents, but all oral commands are also recorded, while more important information is recorded in the operations log. "If commanders of subordinate units took part in the decision-making, the decision is then conveyed orally (at the commander's command post)."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This operations log that is referred to, does it have another name? Or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's not mentioned -- oh, it can be described as a war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you were the author -- or not the author, but the person that recorded entries into the war diary in Vukovar, in the Vukovar operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We'll talk about that war diary a little bit later on, but if we can move now towards the requisites of a command that should be placed in the command, that appears at paragraph 148. And if you can read that out, please, and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't have that paragraph. The last one I have is 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps if I can read out that paragraph, it's in the -- it's in the exhibit in e-court. It states: "A command is a commanding act which categorically and imperatively expresses the commander's decision and concretely, clearly and unambiguously gives tasks to subordinates. "A command for combat operations in principle should include information about the enemy, the brigade's assignment, its reinforcements and support from the superior command, and information about adjacent units and borders with them." And then the commander's decision. Those requirements --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Those requirements for a command as stated in these rules, are they familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain whether or not you believe that -- that aspect of the command or that formulation of the command is -- is important or not, and why?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Orders, as acts of commanding, should contain all of the elements. An order can be in a short written form without all of the elements in particular situations, or in such conditions when one has limited time on his hands, or when it concerns a correction of a previous decision, or if it is a corrective decision by the commander. All of these documents and elements make up the entire process and form of issuing a task or a decision by the commander. And it should contain all of the elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And it appears you don't have this translation of the next paragraph, but if I read it to you, and this is 359: "The brigade commander constantly monitors the situation and influences the course of the battle by issuing new or additional tasks. He makes his decision on the basis of reports submitted by subordinate officers and his personal observations." Is that provision familiar to you, even if you haven't got the translated version in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you have discussed earlier, through other of the rules -- other parts of the rules and regulations of why that, in fact, is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 65 ter number 382, and it's the JNA brigade rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 395, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would just want to ask for a clarification by my learned friend. The excerpts that he wanted to tender and that he used in his examination-in-chief is something that we don't object to, but I just wanted to know whether he would seek to tender the part from which we didn't -- he didn't ask any questions from in examination-in-chief; that is, from paragraph 360 onwards relating to attacks on populated areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Everything that is in this folder is presently exhibited. Mr. Smith has indicated he intends to tender the full document, as I understand it, in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it will become in evidence in due course, but it is not at the moment, except for those few lines on the bottom of the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Your Honour, I will do that at the end of the examination, I will just tender the full manuals completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I believe there is a little confusion. In e-court the excerpts are not included. It's -- there, it's the full document that is in e-court. So my understanding was that each time we were tendering, we were tendering the full document, but what we have in front of us is a reference tool simply for court purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that's not the way I understood your earlier explanation, but it makes the process simpler.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the full document, Mr. Vasic, has now been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if I can ask you to look at tab 5, please. It's 65 ter Exhibit 298. And it relates to the regulations on the application of international laws of war in the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia. And it's issued by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. Do you see the cover page and a few attached pages after?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document in general terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was it in existence in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And we discussed some of the topics here during my education. That is, I wanted to say that we were taught on the subject during our courses there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And without going through provisions word by word, the regulations relate to regulating responsibility of commander's actions for their subordinates at paragraph 21. It relates to liability for criminal responsibility for war crimes and other serious violations via paragraphs 32 and 33 and other provisions. But I would like you to look at paragraph 51, please. And it relates to the duty of members of the armed forces when capturing members of enemy armed forces. And if you have found paragraph 51, I would just ask that you read that paragraph out and then I'll ask one or two questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Duty of the members of the armed forces of the SFRY when capturing members of enemy armed forces. A member of the armed forces of the SFRY shall spare the life of a member of an enemy armed force who surrenders and lays down his arms or is overpowered and shall treat him humanely. Furthermore, he shall prevent him from escaping and take all measures for the prisoner to be taken under guard to a safe place as soon as possible and surrendered to the competent officer. The same treatment shall be accorded to any other person captured in the combat zone. "The establishment of the identity or status of captured members of enemy armed forces is in the competence of specially designated military authorities. "The necessary care and attention shall be extended to the captured wounded and sick. They should be referred to the medical authorities as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything to add to the section in practical terms as to what this duty implies in relation to the protection of captured prisoners? Do you have anything to add to that, or is it self-explanatory enough?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: This rule or this paragraph should be implemented in full. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender Exhibit 298, which is the regulations on the application of the rules of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be Exhibit 396, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we can now look at tab number 6, which is 65 ter number 385, and this the JNA battalion manual for infantry, motorised, mountain, alpine, partisan and marine battalions, dated 1988 with a few excerpts. Are you familiar with this battalion manual?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, was that in existence in -- still in use in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In this manual at paragraph 508, the manual refers to units of a battalion called assault detachments. Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could read out the definition of these assault detachments, it's 508, and then also 509, and then I have a few questions to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. But I don't believe this is the definition itself. This was the way to form or organise such a unit and its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps, then, if you could read it out and give us that information, and then if you can provide a definition in your own terms from your education and experience.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There is a definition, but as far as I can see it doesn't figure here. The assault detachment is a unit of certain size and level containing as much as several companies and battalions with reinforcements, being formed the following reasons. That would be the actual definition. And here it states that: "The assault detachment is formed to carry out an assault on the well-fortified strongholds and in the course of an attack on a populated area in order to capture large and well-fortified buildings and blocks. The battalion is as a rule reinforced with tanks, artillery, engineers and necessary communications equipment. The battalion acting as an assault detachment is specially prepared, trained and drilled for the execution of the task at hand on similar facilities or features."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can ask you a question there.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The reinforcements to a battalion in an assault detachment, would that normally include Territorial Defence in a normal combat situation or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Reinforcements were not supposed to include the TO, but should a TO unit be inside the area of responsibility or -- or of action of the battalion, then combat actions are unified under the command of a single command. In that case, such a TO unit can be resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: We are discussing reinforcements here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There is no mention of resubordination. That is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 509 relates to the tasks of the commander of an assault detachment. Could you read that out, please, and then I may have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "When the commander of the assault detachment receives the task, in addition to the other activities on the preparation and organisation of the attack, he will organise reconnaissance and, in particular, will study the enemy defence system. "The combat disposition of the assault detachment consists of, inter alia, the required number of assault groups, the fire group, the anti-armour group and the reserve. The detachment commander specifies the tasks for the assault groups and other elements of the combat disposition on the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And paragraph 510 provides a definition of assault group. Can you briefly read that out, and then I may have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "The assault group, the size of a reinforced platoon, is formed to carry out an attack on a facility or feature, bunker, building or a part of a bigger building in order to take it, demolish it or neutralise enemy activity, thus making it possible for the detachment to carry out its task."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that will do for the moment. Just one question about the assault detachment relating to the battalion being reinforced, is it the case that the battalion is the -- is the backbone or the main strength of an assault group as a rule, or not? The reason why I ask is that --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is the backbone of the assault detachment and not assault group. Rather, the assault group is the backbone of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I know why my learned friend looked confused. You've cleared that up. Thank you. It was my mistake. Perhaps then if we can talk about the assault group, and in paragraph 510 it says: "The size of a reinforced platoon." Is that the same situation for an assault group, that the platoon in the battalion is the backbone of the assault detachment, and then other units or units are attached? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm familiar with this structure, and the way of forming groups and detachments, an assault group should be the size of a reinforced company and not platoon. We can read here "platoon," hence my question is where is there any mention of company, if an assault detachment is the size of a battalion. Is that a mistake in the rules or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I guess one could have several such assault groups. There are 12 platoons and three companies in a battalion. Therefore, one can have as many as 12 assault groups in one assault detachment, and no mention of a company. I don't understand the text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: But the notion of assault group, that is what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it -- is it your understanding or what was the situation in Vukovar, were there any assault detachments in the -- in the area in which you were in the operational Group South, and were there any assault groups, without stating the names but just whether or not these types of units were present or units were set up.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Assault detachments were formed to be the size of battalion, plus additional reinforcements, as defined here. The composition of assault detachment comprised formation assault groups the size of company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll discuss a little bit more in detail the formation of these groups when we discuss some of the orders which implemented them. But perhaps we'll move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the battalion manual, and it's 65 ter number 385.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the manual will become exhibit number 397.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if I can now ask you to look at tab 7, which is 65 ter number 188. And it relates to the provisional rule on the corps of ground forces. And this rule was brought into being in 1990, April 1990. Are you familiar with this rule or this set of rules in relation to corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just for information, a corps, what is the size of a corps in terms of a unit size in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: A corps is an operations unit. The corps establishment can be adjusted to the circumstances. In the JNA we moved on to the corps formations somewhat later. There used to be a division establishment within the army, but this was a new thing that appeared relating to the formation of corps, as in all other armed forces it is an operational unit, including a certain number of brigades, infantry brigades, armoured mechanised brigades, as well as artillery units, anti-aircraft defence units, depending on its area of activity. That can include the river navy and so on and so forth. This is a higher level operations unit, including several brigades and reinforcements, having its own area of responsibility, and containing elements of the judiciary and investigative organs as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And looking at -- you've probably answered this question, but looking at these rules and the principles contained in them, would they have applied to the guards brigade in 1991, even though we're talking about a brigade, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Guards Motorised Brigade had its own establishment level. You will probably ask me to explain further at a later stage. As for the Operations Group South, it wasn't at the corps level, but approximately at that level, in the operational sense of the word. Because including the guards brigade, there were also some other units and it also enjoyed a certain amount of support, and that was the definition of the Operations Group South. In my view, the corps was not Operations Group South. The group was formed in order to carry out a specific task. Most of the elements comprised therein were the size of a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You -- that's right. In terms of the application of these types of principles relating to corps, are you saying that because operational group south, which we will discuss shortly, was of a similar size to a corps, that these principles would -- would apply because of the similar size? Is that what you're saying, or something different?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The principles applied are to be used for all temporary or interim formations. Operations group is a temporary formation to carry out a specific task. All the principles are used when it comes to corps or interim formations of such composition as discussed here. They are all to be applied in all of those instances equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can look at, say, paragraph 27 of the rule, the paragraph relates to temporary units being formed within corps, namely operative-tactical and tactical groups. Can you read out that paragraph completely, and then I'll have a few questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "As required, temporary units may be established within the corps (operative-tactical and tactical groups). They are formed in exceptional cases, when the corps' zone of action includes clearly separated routes or areas which makes it difficult to ensure unified command and continuous execution of operations. "The composition of an operative-tactical group (OTG) may vary. The group is formed out of units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. In most cases its strength equals several regiments and brigades of various types and a partisan division reinforced with units of artillery, anti-rocket units of the air defence, et cetera, depending on the situation at hand."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the next paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "A tactical group (TG) may have the strength of several battalions of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence reinforced with artillery units, engineers and other units, depending on the assignment."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "In exceptional cases a mixed detachment may be established out of partisan units and units of Territorial Defence, with the necessary reinforcements, and its strength may vary."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. So, from this rule, briefly, what's the difference between the operative-tactical group and the tactical group? What's the main difference between those two groupings?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The main difference is their representative levels. An operative-tactical group has a higher level. It comprises more units, more reinforcements, and it is normally assigned an operation zone. A tactical group has a lower level. It has less units, less battalions. Both apply to both the JNA and the Territorial Defence, needless to say. Therefore, it has a lower level and is itself part of the operative-tactical group during a combat mission. Or perhaps even not. Maybe it has its own independent axis, but that would largely depend on the decision taken by the superior commander. It can be a component of the operative-tactical group, or a temporary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Shortly I will ask you some questions about when the guards brigade went to Vukovar and became a part of operational group south. Operational group south that was set up in the Vukovar area, is that the same as a operative-tactical group, or was it a different type of unit that was being formed?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on their representative establishments it's very difficult for me to draw the distinction. I do believe that it had the level that would correspond to that of an operative-tactical group. In principle, it contained these very elements, nearly all of them, in fact, to a certain degree. So I would deem it to have been an operative-tactical group on the balance. That's what the name seems to imply as well, it's called Operations Group South, if that's what the rule refers to. So that must be it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at chapter III, which is about command and control of this rule. And it relates to -- I understand what you're saying, that this rule relates to corps which haven't come into existence at that stage, at 1990, but in relation to the concept of command and control to large units such as corps, can you read out paragraph 63, please, and explain how command and control applied to military forces of a corps size or something similar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: "Command and control are conscious and organised activities of the corps commander and bodies of command aimed at engaging and unifying the actions and activities of all units, commands, headquarters and other entities of All People's Defence and social self-protection within the zone of operations, as well as all equipment used in combat for the purpose of achieving the said goals in an optimal way. "Command and control are exercised through planning, coordination, organising, command and control, preparation, and execution of operations and other combat actions; they are based on unified, continuous, secure, flexible, effective operative and secret information flows among commands, units and institutions. "The corps commander commands the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence under his command in the zone of operations." Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, thank you. That's fine. In relation to the principles laid out in there in the general provisions on how command and control would apply to a corps, what can you say in relation to the principles applied in the exercise of command and control of Operations Group South when were you in Vukovar? Were the principles the same or different, and if they were different, can you explain how?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were the same. There was no difference whatsoever. All the rules we've looked at, the ones relating to the brigades, the ones relating to the battalion, those are set down by the academy, as well as the ones relating to the corps. The principles are the same across the board. They were the same principles applied back then. Planning, coordination, organising, command and control, these are some of the principles that permeated all the rules governing the work of the armed forces at the time. And the same by extension would seem to apply to the rules in relation to corps. There is not a single rule that does not incorporate these principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that -- for that understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the rules for land forces corps, dated 1990, which is 65 ter number 188, in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 398.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now I would like to turn your mind to the 15th of July --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... On the 15th of July, 1991, you joined the guards brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was transferred directly from the college.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so that we have an understanding of the size of the guards brigade before it went to Vukovar, can you just briefly state the main units that comprised of the guards brigade before they left for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have just referred to the 15th of July. For about 20 days at the time I was not aware of the establishment in Vukovar, and that was in the nature of my work, I got to know all of it immediately. Before its departure for Vukovar, the guards brigade had the structure corresponding to its tasks. I believe it is important to say that. Its principal purpose and task was as follows: To secure persons and features or facilities. Protocol, combat training -- combat use, combat training, as an ongoing activity, and several other auxiliary activities, as it were. In keeping with this principal purpose, a structure was set up in terms of establishment that comprised a brigade command. In principle, this was the same as it normally was in the case of all other brigades, but there were more officers involved in certain sectors or departments, but it had all the other elements. It had the brigade command, and it had a number of units attached to the staff, the brigade staff. It had about eight battalion level units, some involved in combat and some weren't. There were two motorised battalions. Two military police battalions. A battalion that was in charge of securing buildings and facilities. An armoured battalion. A light artillery division of the anti-aircraft defence. And a rear battalion. That was it in terms of how the structure was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it also include an anti-terrorist unit or not? And if it did, what was the size of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The anti-terrorist unit was called in actual fact an anti-terrorist company. It was part of the 1st Battalion. Yes, it did exist, but the name was anti-terrorist company. It had the level of a company, and it was part of the 1st Battalion, establishment-wise, to the best of my recollection. Later on perhaps it became independent. I'm not absolutely positive about this. It was there. It was most probably part of the 1st Battalion, or perhaps at some point it became independent, but I can't quite remember. But it certainly had the level of a company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minor intervention. I think the witness said twice that he believed this unit to have been within the 1st Battalion of the military police, or at least that's what I believe to have heard the witness saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it usual for a brigade, this is back in -- was it usual back in 1991 for a brigade to have two military police battalions? Was that normal?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I talked about the purpose and the tasks. The principal task of the motorised guards brigade was to provide security for persons and facilities or buildings. Then came protocol and everything else. But the principal task was to provide security for persons and buildings. In terms of establishment, I'm saying in order to have this effectively implemented, it was only logical, and after all that's what was eventually decided, for it to have two military police battalions, one of which was used for training purposes, and provided manpower for the 1st Battalion, and these were at this point men who had already been trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimate of the average size of -- of the battalions? You mentioned a number of battalions, two military police, and others, in terms of the numbers of men in each. If you can. If you can't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion, as a matter of principle, and I think the same principle applied to these battalions, this would have comprised over 700 men. The motorised one. 700 each. Police battalions comprised somewhat less. The armoured battalion, a lot less. The rear battalion, well, depending on the logistical needs of the moment, normally between 200 and 300 people. I can't be more specific, but what I'm telling you now is roughly in keeping with the principles that prevailed. With the following proviso: Just before its departure for Vukovar, the unit had both its permanent set-up, as well as the reserve forces, waiting to be mobilised [realtime transcript read in error "motorised"].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you refer to police battalions being somewhat less in size, are you referring to military police battalions?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, military police battalion, the 1st and the 2nd. Establishment-wise, within the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that military police battalions were somewhat less, about how much less? Can you approximate or not with any sort of reasonable accuracy?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: A reasonable ballpark figure, establishment-wise, would be about 300 up to 400 rear units. Well, a total of about 400 or 450 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned that the military police battalion's role in -- before Vukovar was to secure persons and buildings. When you say secure persons, what type of people were they securing before Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be very specific, I'm afraid, about persons. I didn't have the time to go into that. Military persons, high-ranking military officials probably, but I'm not positive. But they certainly did provide security for all the buildings, all the important features, the General Staff, the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence. The retired JNA generals were entitled to a certain level of protection, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time for the break, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is that. Line 70 -- page 78, line 6, should the word "motorised" be mobilised or mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That would seem logical, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume just after 10 past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before we had the break we discussed or you discussed the task that the military police battalions had before they arrived in Vukovar. I would now like to ask you: From the time that you arrived in the guards brigade in July 1991 until the time that you left for Vukovar with the guards brigade, did the size of the guards brigade increase, or was it reinforced at all with reserves?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And by the time that the guards brigade left for Vukovar, about what percentage of the troops, the people within the brigade, were reservists, compared to professionals or the conscripts that had been conscripted earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really specify, but according to the principles of the replenishment of units, classification A, it should be a percentage of up to 20 per cent. The reservists were used to replenish all units that were part of the combat establishment that had reserve forces according to the combat establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And we'll be looking at some documents in a moment, but just to provide an overview for the Court, what date did the guards brigade leave and head to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How much of the guards brigade went to the Vukovar operations? Was it all or part of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade without the security battalion, and some people who didn't feel fit, who were sick. I mean soldiers and officers and also some people who needed to stay in order to implement tasks and duties in the barracks. It was a small number of people who remained in these tasks. The most part of the staff that remained were those who were in the security battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "the security battalion," are you referring to one of the military police battalions, or are you referring to another battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am not speaking about the battalion I mentioned in the organisation and structural battalion. The security battalion was a special-purpose one. It secured facilities that were also in the jurisdiction of the guards brigade, as well as a number of buildings that housed institutions of the federal ministry and the General Staff. The Federal Secretariat and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the military police battalions, the two that you referred to earlier, they went to Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you may have mentioned this earlier, but what was the date that the guards brigade came back from Vukovar after the operation there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When -- when the battalion left for Vukovar, can you give a reasonably accurate figure as to the number of people, the number of troops in the battalion, officers and regular soldiers and staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion. You asked me about the battalion. Is that what you meant? Or the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. That's -- that's my mistake. The brigade. The guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot give you a precise, an exact number. The battalions that had been replenished up to the establishment number of about 700 men altogether, but I really cannot tell you exactly. I think the number was somewhere in the range of 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What reputation did the guards brigade have before Vukovar commenced, in comparison to other brigades in relation to the -- the quality of their performance and the quality of personnel in the brigade generally? Did it have a reputation and, if it did, what was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Its reputation was -- had more weight than most of the other units in the Yugoslav People's Army. And the reputation was a result of the purpose and the tasks it had. They were responsible and had to do with the most important tasks of security and protocol of the top state and military leadership. As far as I can recall, it was directly under the federal secretary's Chief of Staff. As far as the personnel is concerned, the Guards Motorised Brigade has a long-standing tradition, since 1945, and throughout its whole history it took care of the most important security tasks. Even at one period it was entrusted with the security of the president of the SFRY. And ever since that period the reputation and the rating of the guards brigade kept growing. As far as personnel is concerned, the guards brigade consisted only of people who met certain criteria, and the criteria were very strict. When we're talking about officers and civilians, when we're talking about soldiers, they were criteria which were also quite strict for them in all aspects; security, health, physical looks, commitment. And ultimately I think that nobody could become a member of the guards brigade without expressing the wish to do that and without being ready to carry out the tasks that they were informed about when they requested or were proposed for a member of the guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the guards brigade reputation have any impact on the amount and type of, say, combat equipment that it was issued with, or was it similar to -- to other brigades in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, the equipment was -- depended on the objectives, the purpose and the assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: For a particular objective, appropriate equipment and weapons would be issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when the -- when the brigade, and we're talking perhaps now in overview terms, because we have these documents we'll go through for specifics. But in broad context when the guards brigade went to the area of Vukovar, did it become subordinate to another command or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was immediately subordinated to the command of Operations Group South, which was under the command of Colonel Bajo Bojat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just briefly, for about how long was the guards brigade under the command of Colonel Bojac [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Bajo Boja [phoen]. About 10 days. Since I was reading the war diary last night, actually it was on the 8th of October that the transfer was effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was that transfer?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The superior command decided that the guards brigade should take over the responsibility for the zone of operations and that the guards brigade command should be transformed into the command of Operations Group South. I don't know, I didn't see that document by the superior command, but that's how it should have been, according to the line of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then who was the -- who then logically was the commander of operational group south?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The zone of operations was taken over by the Guards Motorised Brigade, and the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade transformed itself into the command of Operations Group South, and the then commander, Mile Mrksic, was appointed as commander of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who did the command of operational group south, who did that command report to? What was the next level up?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the commander of --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: According to the orders of the federal secretary, it was subordinated to the command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was the command of the 1st -- in command of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: General Zivota Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the area of the 1st Military District, what did that include, what was the size of it? Just in approximate terms. Just very generally.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot make a precise estimate. At the time the entire territory of the SFRY was divided into military districts. As far as I know, the Ljubljana region was abolished and that left the 1st Belgrade, the 3rd Skoplje, the 5th Zagreb Districts. It covered a lot of territory, but this had nothing to do with a state or administrative borders. It was covering the area of Eastern Slavonia, perhaps all the way to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the -- the 1st Military District, the commander, General Panic, who was his superior, who did he report to? Which was the next -- what was the next level up, militarily?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the General Staff in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In operational group south in general terms, once the guards brigade command took command of the operational group, what other units were in that operational group in addition to the guards brigade? So we're talking now, perhaps, mid-October? In general terms. We'll look at the documents in a moment.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In mid-October, I think that the following units were attached: Part of the artillery units of the 1st Military District; the 20th Partisan Brigade was also part of the operations group, it joined them around the 15th; then also parts of the mechanised or armoured, of the mechanised brigade from Sremska Mitrovica; and I think the territorial units in Vukovar and in the surrounding villages. I am not sure specifically what the situation was on the 15th of October. I'm sure about the units that I mentioned, but perhaps there were some other units, volunteer units, but I really cannot remember right now which ones they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps if we can look at Exhibit 103, please. Witness, what you will see on the screen will be a map of Eastern Croatia, it will come up shortly, it's not in your documents there. And it will show a map of that particular area. When you see the map on the screen, with the assistance of the usher, please, I would ask you to draw the general area of operational group south so that we can see the approximate size of it. And if possible, if we -- thank you, that's good. Perhaps if we could go one level higher too, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's fine. It's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, the usher will give you a magical pen which can draw on the computer screen. And before you start to draw if you can take your time and draw the area that operational group south covered, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. There is one place that is not shown here, and that's where the logistics of the operations group was. That's the village of Berak. So I think that was in the area of Grabovo, somewhere nearby. So for that part I'm not sure if I'm going to be quite precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it the case that Grabovo was located in operational group south or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Berak was part of it. I think that they kind of bordered on one another. That would be it. Grabovo, Grabovo would be to the east, if Berak is to the west of it, as I think that it is. [Marks]. There you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So does that reflect the zone of responsibility of operational group south; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I would have to provide additional explanations about this zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can briefly provide that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The operations zone of Operations Group South is the town of Vukovar up to River Vuka, within the boundaries, the mouth of the Vuka River into the Danube to the east or to the right. The River Danube, including the places Ovcara, Jakubovac, which are not on the map, but they are on a -- on a different map. It also includes Negoslavci and Berak. To the west or to the left you have the River Vuka ruling -- or excluding Nustar, Petrovci, Mirkovci, and excluding Stari Jankovci. Therefore, the operations zone is elongated because of the deployment of the logistics units of Operations Group South. The front is as follows: Along the outskirts of the town, encompassing the width of the town, the north boundary or the line which was supposed to have been reached was the River Vuka. These are the required explanations for the way the zone looks. It is deeper and not as wide. We're talking about an attack of the town, operation on the town with elements to the depth which were essential and which were as they were in the operations principles and that is how they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the size of the operations group, from north to south about how many kilometres would it be, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: About 14 kilometres to Berak, up to the front line. That would be the depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, say, from east to west, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The width was eight kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And we'll discuss the particular units that were operating within the zone of responsibility of operational group south shortly, but approximately how many other troops were present in that operational zone, say, mid-October? You said that the guards brigade had approximately 4.000 that left for Vukovar. What would be the total size of the troops operating in that zone in mid-October, not including the guards brigade? A rough figure.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: The military situation was changing. Only from the 15th of October did it begin to grow. But I don't think that it was, as far as the force was concerned, any more than by one-third, in comparison to the strength at the beginning of the operation. I'm saying changeable because some units were leaving and others were joining the forces, so in this time period from the 15th of October until the 11th the strength did increase by about 50 per cent in relation to the previous situation, but this was not something that happened every day. Some forces were leaving, some were coming. So if we're talking about 50 per cent, then we're talking about possibly up to 6.000. At one point, when the 20th Partisan Brigade left, the strength dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, briefly, when did the 20th Partisan Brigade leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: It arrived on the 15th, and based on the decision by the government, they were supposed to be there for some 40 days. I believe they were relieved after 40 days. That is, the 15th of November. It must have been before the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so, say, before the 20th of November, say the 18th of November, for argument's sake, what would have been the size of the guards brigade relative to the other troops in the area? I know you can't be precise, but at least if you can give us an estimation.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: They left, and between the 15th of November up to the 18th, as far as I can remember, no other unit replaced it. Therefore, the manning strength should be reduced by the size of that brigade. Although it wasn't a classical size brigade, it was a partisan brigade, and it may have had around 1.000 to 1200 troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in relation to the numbers, you mentioned about 4.000 guards brigades -- I'm sorry, 4.000 troops within the guards brigade. About how many others at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Around 4.000, and there were 2.000 of them. Not at the same time though, but interchangeably, as was dictated by the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If could you mark that circle with a number 1 to identify operational group south zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With exhibit number 399, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can also ask for Exhibit 156, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Witness, the map that will be produced on the screen will be more of a detailed map of the Vukovar township area and the surrounds. And it won't contain the full area of operational group south, but at least if you could put the borders of that -- of that group, draw them on the map, that would be useful. Thank you. Witness, would you like the map enlarged one further level?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can go back to the original version, and then from, say, just above the hospital, if we could have to the bottom of the -- bottom of the map. Right to the bottom. Thank you. Witness, do you recognise this map? I mean there are some photos added on to it, but the map generally?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Would you able -- are you able to draw the boundaries, as best you can, of operational group south zone of responsibility with the pen, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid the witness didn't quite understand the map. In the previous exhibit, 544 -- I'm sorry, 399, the witness said that the boundary was on the River Vuka, but obviously on this map he hasn't found the river. Perhaps my learned friend could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That may clear up things, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at that map, I think previously you said that the northern border of the operational group south's zone of responsibility was the Vuka River; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you look closely at the map, where it's stated Nova Ulica, are you able to see the river as it heads out towards the Danube, just above that area?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Just above where it says Dunav.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm wearing glasses and I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nor can I, and I think the witness, understandably, would have difficulty as well. I'm going to suggest that we lose what has been marked so far, enlarge the area of Vukovar itself once more, and allow the witness to orient himself. I'm sure if it becomes something that can be seen his experience will enable him to identify features.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's a good idea. If it could be enlarged say at least maybe two levels so that the Vuka River can be seen, and then we can go to the smaller level once he's oriented himself. Perhaps even one level again. I think that will do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, we can go to another level again, but do you see -- do you see the river, or we'll enlarge the town. Perhaps if we can enlarge it one level again, please. Just right close in on the town, please. I think that will do. Thank you. Thank you. Witness, are you able to see the river there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could just point it with the marking pen, thanks.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It goes around, there is a bend here. It goes just above the hospital. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just -- just to let you know, witness, the river doesn't go up that high. But where you have the lowest point of the red line, that, in fact, is where the river is, and it continues across with a light blue line towards the Danube. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Smith, what appears to be a river can also be seen where the witness has marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Part of the problem may be the detail, or lack of it, in this depiction on the screen. I can understand why the witness has drawn the line where he has, but whether that is the correct position is another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right. Okay. I agree. Perhaps, then, if we can go back to the original -- the original map. I believe -- I believe if we enlarge right in on the centre of town where the river is the witness will be able to see it. And perhaps then we can have a correct drawing. Thank you. Stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you see -- do you see the hospital at the top, the red dot, and if you go further down --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- to the right, just underneath it, you see the words "Vuka" in blue. Now are you familiar enough with the map to see that that's the Vuka River or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
