utterances.text: I saw that it was the River Vuka. But the city hospital was within the area of responsibility of Operations Group South, because this part of the Vuka -- or is this a part of a lake? That was the upper limit, the upper boundary, towards the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Smith, if the witness is confident of the depiction on the map, he should mark what he suggests is the area of responsibility of Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can now go back to the map in its original form, and if we can just I think that's -- perhaps just one level up, please. And to the bottom, thank you. Actually, that's my mistake, if we can go back to the original map and try to have the witness mark the area, if we go back to the original level. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, now looking at the map, as best you can, can you draw the area of responsibility of operational group south, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you place the number 1 within the area that you have depicted as the zone of responsibility for operational group south?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the headquarters, the operational group south headquarters, where were they located?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Should I mark it on the map? Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that flag symbol is a symbol for the headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, as far as the -- that area within the area of operational group south --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's zone of operations, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that correct? The area that you have depicted, is that the zone of operations of operational group south?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. The zone of operations of operational group south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at what time period was that the zone of operations? Was that for the whole time that the guards brigade was there, or sometime less?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I seek to tender that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked map will become Exhibit 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mentioned that the headquarters of operational group south was at Negoslavci, and during the period of time that the guards brigade were in Vukovar, what was your job? What was your function?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I've already mentioned that I was senior officer with the department for operations and training or education upon the department's head -- when the department's head left, and that was Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic. Based on oral orders by Chief of Staff, probably with the approval of Lieutenant-Colonel Mrksic, I also carried out the tasks of the head of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that with -- it was with the approval of Lieutenant-Colonel Mrksic. Was that the correct rank that he had at that stage?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was my immediate superior. Based on Lieutenant-Colonel's -- Lieutenant-Colonel Panic's orders, and based on the approval of Lieutenant-Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: There was no written document confirming that, but in the absence of the chief the senior officer can carry out such tasks, that was according to regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And approximately what date was that that you carried out the tasks of the head of operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Head of operations organ, not of operations, strictly speaking. I can't be precise, but some three or four days after the commencement of operations, I presume it was around the 3rd, the 4th or the 5th of October, at the very beginning, a few days later, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And in a -- in a practical sense, what -- what would your day entail? Were you based at the headquarters, did you go out to the combat area, and at what -- practically, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As part of the organ for operations and education, apart from the chief who was given another assignment, there were five to six operatives. As the senior officer in charge of administration, I was supposed to take over the duties prescribed for that particular position. But in carrying out the tasks of the chief the nature of the situation and the circumstances dictated that I spent more time at the command or, rather, at the staff of the command to monitor the situation, to receive reports, to be present at briefings, to participate in proposing measures and decisions together with the other command -- brigade command officers based on the principle used in the process of decision-making. Because of that, I seldom went to the immediate combat area or, rather, to the front lines. I remember that after having been issued with tasks by the commander of the guards brigade, Colonel Mrksic, and at the beginning that wasn't operations group, and I was present when the tasks were issued near Vukovar and that one or two days after the combat commenced, together with Colonel Pavkovic and Major Sljivancanin, I was at the barracks in Vukovar. Then we went on to Petrova Gora to see the commander of the assault detachment number 1. I remember that on several other occasions I toured the units on the outskirts of Vukovar, first and foremost at Mitnica, I was there with the Chief of Staff. Perhaps I was in the barracks on one other occasion, but I can't be precise as to the date. And on the 22nd or the 23rd I was in Vukovar with Colonel Pavkovic. Since I was permanently at the staff, he thought that it would be good for me to see the situation on the ground. Otherwise, I was completely at the staff, at the command post in the operations room carrying out the aforementioned duties, together with other senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just so that we can get a clear picture, approximately what percentage of your time was spent in the headquarters versus being out in the combat area? Are we talking a small percentage or something larger?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: I spent a small percentage of time within the combat area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said earlier that at one stage you were the senior officer in charge of administration. Is that correct or has it been misrecorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: For operational issues, the most senior officer in the operations department is charged with monitoring situation, collecting data, making assessments, so that he could present such data to his chief, and that was me at certain point, being the senior officer, and together with the other most senior officers, we dealt with decision-making. In the decision-making process, all staff organs are included as well as all the aspects of the armed forces, and the operations organ headed by myself at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to get a picture of what your work was like, the headquarters at Negoslavci, what type of building was that and about how much staff were attached to the command, the OG South command, in terms of working within that location?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, a command post has three or four separate elements. The operations part, the aspects parts, the group for assistance, the communications group. Given the situation at Negoslavci, we adjusted to the conditions there. It was a house of a local who had left Negoslavci, and he put it at our disposal. It had a large living room, quite long and narrow, and it served as an operations room. According to their tasks, basically all of the command organs were there. The brigade commander had a separate small room to rest, and a side room in which he could have meetings, provided they didn't include large numbers of people. And there was a corridor and a terrace. That's as far as the working space was at the command post. When it comes to the rest for the personnel, in Negoslavci there was another house and rest and accommodation for the officers were secured there, provided they were not at the command doing their tasks. The communications centre and the assistance group assisting the command, they were in some other basements or the outhouses, and out in the open. Basically the conditions for work at the command post were quite poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At the house where the command was working from, the brigade command, I mean the OG South command, about how many -- how many staff of that command would be working in that house at any one time? I know it changed -- it would have changed over time, but approximately how many people would work, say, in that command house on any given day?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, right from the outset people took shifts. There were tasks that had to be carried out. People needed to rest. And further, there had to be constant monitoring of units in the area of combat operations. If everybody from the brigade command happened to be in that small operations room at the same time, there was no way the room could have held them, those 30 people from the inner circle of the leadership, as it were. However, people took shifts. The commander would always send some officers, and this was in keeping with the principle of inspection. He would send these officers to tour the units and help them out. Some of them went deep into the territory to visit the auxiliary units and the rear units in order to see if they could give them a hand. But some officers stayed right there. It was in the same building that we had a communications centre for the signals people. All the information was received there, and you could listen to all the information being exchanged with any of the units or with the superior command whenever there were incoming calls with requests for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. So on average, if 30 -- if 30 inner circle of the leadership of the command staff would not be there in the command house at any one time, approximately what number would be there throughout the period at any one time? Would it be half that amount or over or under?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 men most of the time. And also, when briefings took place, the regular ones, the inner circle belonging to the command, as it were, and the unit commanders, that those would add up to, roughly speaking, a total of 15 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You said earlier that part of -- one of your jobs was to receive reports, and also propose measures and assisting them in the decision-making. Does that mean that you, in fact, recorded in some way of document the orders that had come in to the headquarters from other places? Was that one of your jobs, to record those?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of my duties. I had to use the war diary as envisaged by the principals to enter the most important orders that had never been received in written form, active orders received from our superior command and such documents as any reports from our subordinate units. Likewise, observations were entered made by officers carrying out rounds of inspection in units along the front line in Vukovar. Other types of information were recorded too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This war diary, would -- is it fair to say that that is -- it was -- its purpose was to be a comprehensive account of important events occurring in the operational group zone and of important orders coming in, important reports coming in and going out, such that when the commander or someone who needed to had to look at what the situation was in operational group south, they would have a good overview of significant events and activities? Is that reasonable?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In terms of a document that's the most comprehensive of important matters such as we've just talked about, is the war diary the most comprehensive overview of day-to-day important events and decisions and orders? Or is there another document that is more comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as events were concerned about which there was nothing in writing, I think the war diary is probably the most reliable source, and the most comprehensive source. However, when talking about documents that were written, files on these documents that were kept are probably the most comprehensive source in relation to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say those files on the documents kept are probably the most comprehensive, do you mean comprehensive in terms of the amount of detail they contain, or comprehensive in the amount of separate and singular incidents and -- that they may cover?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: For example, if there is a written document, be it an order by a superior command, or a report drafted by one of the subordinate officers, it is not necessarily entered into the war diary, just by virtue of being what it is. But once it was assigned a number, it had to be entered into the register of the general administration office. This register contains all the documents that were received from any level at all, higher up or lower down. Some of those documents were marked in the war diary too. But everything else that was not received in writing but was known about based on reports from the inspection officers, based on the reports of officers through our communications equipment, based on information provided by our subordinate officers, based on information received by the duty officer, at a time when the operations officers were not there, well, all of this had to be entered into the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the register you talk about that was kept to record incoming -- I think you may have said incoming reports and orders, and -- or any document that was incoming, is it the case that that had to record every one, every written order and report, as a matter of protocol?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every report and every order received from the superior command had to be entered into the register. The register which contained our documents. There was no register kept in our subordinate units, not all of them at any rate, as far as I remember. Therefore, such information and such documents as were received by the brigade command would not be registered in any of the lower-level units. However, I think most of the information and documents received from the lower-level units were eventually registered in this register book. When somebody drafts a document and this document is sent to the general administration office, it is entered into the register and forwarded to whoever it's addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So on that basis, does this register also record all outgoing reports and documents, reports and orders, as well as incoming, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, of course, we're referring to written reports and orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know I'm about two minutes short, but it seems like an appropriate time to break in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- the topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then adjourn for the day. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning because we are not able to sit in the afternoon, as the courtroom will be used by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
